BKNG · Earnings robustness report · data through Q3 2026 (filed Nov 3, 2026) · Nov 23, 2026

How robust are Booking’s earnings?

Income, shares, and what the market pays for earnings stay on the key-metrics page.

Robust. Booking earns more each year mainly because more people book more nights through it, and because it now handles the payment on most of them. Over the last twelve months operating income, excluding a one-off FTC charge, rose about 20% and free cash flow reached $9.2B, about 1.3 times reported profit.

Buybacks help, but they are not the engine. They supplied about a third of adjusted EPS growth over the past decade and over the last year. That pace now has to come from cash flow rather than new debt, because leverage is at the company’s own ceiling. At today’s share price, cash flow alone still buys back roughly 7% of the company a year.

The cracks are at the edges. Q4 volume growth slows to 1–3%. The FTC bill is $1.0B so far and could grow. Marketing per room night and IT costs, which include AI, are rising faster than revenue. Vayo’s planned $100M is about 1% of a year’s profit, too small to matter.

1 · Where the profit growth comes from

More nights, worth more each, with Booking increasingly taking the payment. The take rate settled near 14–14.5% after 2021. The fourth-quarter guide is room nights up 1–3%, and gross bookings up 2–4% as reported or 4–6% in constant currency.

Has the buyback strategy changed?

The words have not changed; the pace has. 2026 brought two record quarters, $3.6 billion and then $3.7 billion, the second funded partly with $3 billion of new debt, then a slower third quarter at $2.1 billion. The board also raised the quarterly dividend 9.4%, to $0.42 after the 25-for-1 split. With leverage at the company’s own ceiling, future buybacks track cash flow.

Q4 2025 call · Feb 18, 2026 · CFO Ewout Steenbergen
“Since restarting our repurchase program in early 2022, following the pandemic related pause, we have returned over 100% of free cash flow to shareholders, repurchasing $29 billion in stock and driving a 22% reduction in share count net of the dilutive effect of stock-based compensation. Going forward, we plan to continue to return capital to our shareholders as well as maintain our disciplined focus on optimizing our capital structure, built on a foundation of investment grade credit ratings and around 2x growth leveraged through the cycle.”
The transcript reads "2x growth leveraged"; that is almost certainly "gross leverage".
Q1 2026 call · Apr 28, 2026 · CEO Glenn Fogel
“...the record $3.6 billion in share repurchases we completed in the first quarter. Since 2014, we have reduced our share count by over 40%, even after accounting for the dilutive impact of stock-based compensation by opportunistically investing in this long-term vision through our share buyback program. ... we have done so at the average price per share of $93 ... It is a strategy that we are very committed to.”

4 · Is spending creeping up?

Marketing is the cost to watch. It has fallen as a share of revenue and bookings, but per room night it rose about 7% over the last year, driven by B2B affiliates. Capex is tiny, and AI sits in IT expense, not capex.

AI spend: what is and isn’t disclosed

No filing gives an AI dollar figure. IT expense carries it: $302 million in the third quarter, up 25%. On the fourth-quarter 2025 call the CFO said 2026 reinvestment above the baseline is about $700 million, including generative AI, and that the company expenses the cost rather than capitalizing it.

Q2 2026 call · Aug 4, 2026 · CFO
“...if I'm looking specifically about our AI costs, yes, they're going up. It could be token costs or license fees. It's still at a low single digit level of our overall technology spend.”
Q3 2026 call · Nov 3, 2026 · CFO
“...marketing rose, driven primarily by faster growth in B2B affiliate marketing expenses.” The consumer business, he said, had marketing leverage.

Follow-up questions

What a careful investor would ask next, answered from filings and calls where possible.

If the FTC asks for more than the $1.0B accrual, what does it cost?
Booking has booked $1.0B and says the FTC “may seek monetary penalties and restitution in excess of these amounts”. It gives no range. Each extra $1B would be about 11% of a year’s free cash flow and $1.33 a share before tax, about 13% of a year’s adjusted EPS. It would be a one-time hit, and none of it is paid yet.
The 10-Q says the FTC may ask for more than the $1 billion already booked, and it gives no range.
Can buybacks keep this pace if free cash flow flattens?
Not with more debt. Gross debt is $20.1B against $10.7B of trailing adjusted EBITDA, 1.87x. In November the company issued €3.55 billion of senior notes, stated in euros as filed, and $1.99 billion of debt is due within a year. Management’s target is “around 2x” gross leverage. This page does not convert the euro notes into dollars. Net debt is only $4.2B (0.4x) because Booking holds $15.8B of cash, but part of that cash is customers’ prepayments ($6.45B of deferred merchant bookings). $12.4B of authorization is left. From here, buybacks grow only as fast as cash flow and EBITDA.
Debt, cash, and the buyback authorization left are from the filings. The November notes are stated in euros, as filed.
How much EPS growth is left if buybacks are funded by free cash flow alone?
Quite a lot, because the stock is cheaper. TTM free cash flow minus dividends is $7.95B. At the Nov 19 close of $147.32 that retires about 54M shares, 7.2% of the count, before employee stock (SBC is about 0.6% of market value a year). The last twelve months’ $12.0B bought back about 11% of today’s market value but cut the average share count only 5.1%. The difference is price and timing: H1 buybacks averaged about $173 a share. A cash-funded pace still adds roughly 5–7 points a year to EPS, if the price stays near here.
The shares this cash could retire are illustrative at the November 19 close, not a forecast.
What is behind the Q4 slowdown? Brands, regions, price or volume?
Volume, mostly. The fourth-quarter guide is room nights up 1–3%. Gross bookings are guided up 2–4% as reported and 4–6% in constant currency. Management attributes the gap to higher constant-currency room rates and more flight tickets. It cites the toughest comparison of 2026, Middle East disruption, high airfares and unrest in some European cities, and expects FX to cut reported growth by about 2 points. Booking gives region color only for the third quarter: Europe and Asia high single digits, the US and Rest of World mid single digits. There is no split by brand (Booking.com vs Priceline, Agoda and the others).
The guide and the call explain the slowdown; Booking does not split it by brand.
Marketing per room night is rising. Is that paid search getting more expensive?
The filings point elsewhere. On the Q3 call the CFO said marketing rose 11%, “driven primarily by faster growth in B2B affiliate marketing expenses”, while the consumer (B2C) business “had marketing leverage”. That means marketing grew slower than bookings there. The direct-relationship metrics are improving: B2C direct mix is stable in the mid-60% range, the app’s share of room nights rose from the mid-50% to the high-50% range, and Genius Level 2 and 3 members (the top tiers of Booking.com’s loyalty program) make up a high-50% share of Booking.com room nights, up on last year. The split between performance and brand marketing has not been published since 2019.
The call points to affiliate marketing; the filings do not split performance and brand.
Is AI showing up in the numbers yet?
On costs, yes, modestly. Customer-service costs fell in Q3 “despite higher booking volumes”. Sales and other expenses were 2.0% of gross bookings and a source of leverage. Adjusted fixed costs rose only 6%, with personnel slightly down. On revenue, not yet: referrals from AI chatbots are “significantly less than 1%” of Booking.com room nights. On spend, IT expense, which carries AI costs, grew 25% in Q3.
From the third-quarter call and the 10-Q.
How sensitive are earnings to interest rates?
Mildly. Over the last twelve months interest income was $0.81B and interest expense $1.11B, so net interest was −$0.31B. Each 1-point change in the yield on $15.8B of cash moves pre-tax income by about $0.16B, $0.21 a share or about 2% of adjusted EPS. The new notes carry fixed coupons (3.95–5.0%). FY2025 interest expense included non-cash convertible-note charges.
The interest lines are from the filings; the rate sensitivity is on the cash balance.
Is the tax rate creeping up?
A little. The effective rate was about 19–22% from 2021 to 2025 and is 22.1% for the first nine months of 2026, against 20.0% a year earlier. The 10-Q blames a valuation allowance on US interest carryforwards and discrete items. The Netherlands Innovation Box still lowers the rate. The spikes in 2017 (US tax reform) and 2020 (losses) are one-offs.
The rate is tax divided by pre-tax income, from the filings.
Does stock compensation eat the buybacks?
No. Stock comp was $613M in FY2025, about 9.5% of the $6.44B spent on buybacks. Booking also paid $530M to withhold employees’ shares for their taxes. In 2025 the company issued 245,000 shares before the split, 6.125 million after it, for option exercises and vested awards, including 148,431 restricted shares and 86,213 performance shares (5.866 million after the split). The same line was 228,000 shares in 2024 and 267,000 in 2023. Net of all that, the diluted share count still fell 4.2% in 2025 and 5.1% over the last twelve months. Management counts stock comp as a cost in its adjusted EPS.
Stock pay and buybacks are both from the cash-flow statement.
How bad does a downturn get? The 2020 test
Bad for one year, then fast back. In 2020 revenue fell 55% and marketing fell 56%, because most of it is performance marketing (89% in 2019), which falls when searches fall. The other costs only fell 12%. Operating income was −$0.63B, or +$0.43B before a $1.06B goodwill write-down, and adjusted EPS fell 95%. Free cash flow was −$0.2B, but the cause was $2.3B of customer prepayments unwinding. Without that it was +$2.1B. Deferred merchant bookings were $1,561 million at the end of 2019 and $323 million at the end of 2020, against $6.45 billion on September 30, 2026. Buybacks stopped after Q1. By 2023 operating income and adjusted EPS were back above 2019. Today the float at risk is larger ($6.45B of deferred merchant bookings), but so are the cash and the profit cushion.
2020 is from that year’s 10-K, including the goodwill write-down.

Gaps

  • Booking has not printed a performance-versus-brand marketing split since 2019, so marketing is one combined line.
  • Marketing per room night uses all marketing over all room nights, because Booking does not print a consumer-only marketing figure.
  • Booking does not print an AI dollar figure. The only number management has given is that AI costs are a low-single-digit share of technology spend.
  • Booking does not split capital spending by purpose. Capitalized software was $1,437 million at the end of 2025, up from $1,249 million, with no AI split.
  • No SEC filing names Vayo, so the amount, timing, and accounting of the planned $100 million are undisclosed.
  • Adjusted earnings per share are not defined the same way every year, so that history is not perfectly like for like.
  • The 2020–2022 earnings-per-share split is blank because pandemic earnings were near zero, which makes the split meaningless.
  • The cash-flow statement shows $6.44 billion of 2025 repurchases; the call said $5.9 billion. This page uses the cash-flow line.
  • The $1.0 billion FTC accrual is unpaid, and Booking has not said when the cash will go out.
  • Booking does not give a range for what the FTC may seek above the $1.0 billion already booked.
  • Booking reports one segment and does not print room nights or revenue by brand. Region color is given for the third quarter only.
  • Management says affiliate marketing drove the third-quarter increase, but it does not print the affiliate dollars.
Sources: Booking’s 10-K, 10-Q, earnings releases and call transcripts, and the November 2026 notes prospectus. Not investment advice.
